extracted.intended_audience: researchers, science policy makers, and stakeholders interested in NIH peer review and funding disparities
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of NIH R01 applications using the five standard reviewer criterion scores (Significance, Investigators, Innovation, Approach, Environment) and the Overall Impact score, with attention to how criterion scoring relates to racial disparities in outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of NIH's five criterion scores used by reviewers to judge how important the proposed research problem is. The study found Black applicants received worse scores on this criterion (as on all five criteria), contributing to overall impact disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualifications and experience of the investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates the research team's expertise, track record, and capacity to carry out the project. Identified as one of the five criterion scores where Black applicants received systematically worse scores even after controlling for applicant and application characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses whether the proposed research uses novel ideas or methods. The paper reports a consistent Black–White gap in Innovation scores, indicating bias operating at the criterion scoring level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges the rigor and feasibility of the study design, methods, and planned analyses. Approach scores were among the criterion scores that differed by applicant race, contributing to disparities in Overall Impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers whether the institutional setting, facilities, and support are adequate to ensure project success. The study found worse Environment scores for Black applicants, part of the multi-criterion source of disparity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Impact score
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary impact assessment on a 1–9 scale (1 = best).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An aggregated overall impact score used in NIH peer review. Key finding: differences in the five criterion scores fully account for the Black–White gap in Overall Impact scores — reviewers did not differentially weight criteria by applicant race.

rubrics_metrics.name: Component-level scoring bias (rubric-design implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias operates at the level of how each criterion is individually scored rather than in how criteria are combined/weighted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: interventions should target how reviewers judge each criterion (perception/judgment) rather than only changing how criterion scores are aggregated. Removing or de-emphasizing any single criterion is unlikely to eliminate disparities because the gap is present across all criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency via criterion structure is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of the five-criterion structure (2009) did not reduce racial disparities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides rubric designers and policymakers that simply adding structured criteria for transparency does not prevent biased scoring; additional measures addressing reviewer judgment on each component are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pre-discussion reviewer scores to isolate rubric application
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological approach: analyze preliminary (pre-discussion) individual reviewer scores to separate rubric-application from group deliberation effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice for studies of review bias: use pre-discussion scores to focus on the step where reviewers apply criterion rubrics individually, since this isolates the contribution of component scoring to overall disparities.
